value_proposition: Build and deploy commercially useful, fault-tolerant quantum computers using a manufacturable, modular silicon-photonics platform that leverages semiconductor foundries, telecom fiber networking, integrated control systems, and purpose-built FTQC software.
target_customers: Organizations in energy, materials, pharmaceuticals, and finance
qubit_modality: Dual-rail photonic qubits implemented on a silicon-photonics platform, with on-chip single-photon sources and superconducting single-photon detectors.
computing_models: Photonic quantum computing using two-qubit fusion operations
hardware_architecture: A modular architecture progressing from 300 mm wafers to chips, packages, blades, cabinets, and complete quantum computers. The Omega chipset integrates single-photon sources, superconducting single-photon detectors, interferometric/optical components, edge couplers, and high-performance optical switches on an ultra-low-loss silicon-nitride platform. Modules are intended to network over standard telecom optical fiber, with control electronics integrated near the qubits in modular packaging.
current_systems: Omega silicon-photonic chipset/platform manufactured in a commercial semiconductor foundry

Demonstrated integrated photonic components and benchmark operations, including qubit initialization/readout, interference between independent photon sources, chip-to-chip transmission, and two-qubit fusion
No completed utility-scale quantum computer is identified in the supplied material
one_qubit_fidelity: 99.98% ± 0.01% single-qubit SPAM fidelity. This is an initialization-and-readout metric, not a disclosed one-qubit gate fidelity.
two_qubit_fidelity: 99.22% ± 0.12% two-qubit fusion fidelity, described as validating entangling-operation accuracy.
connectivity: Demonstrated chip-to-chip qubit transmission over optical fiber at 99.72% ± 0.04% fidelity. The proposed scaling architecture connects modules using standard telecom optical fiber without transduction. System-scale connectivity topology and fan-out are not disclosed.
fault_tolerance_strategy: The platform is explicitly designed for fault-tolerant quantum computing and combines photonic chips, fusion-based entangling operations, networking, cryogenics, controls, and FTQC software. However, the supplied material does not disclose the error-correcting code, threshold, physical-to-logical overhead, decoding implementation, or a demonstrated fault-tolerant logical operation.
roadmap: Scale the modular silicon-photonics platform from chips and packages into blades, cabinets, and utility-scale quantum computers
Build the first planned utility-scale sites in the City of Moreton Bay, Queensland, Australia, and Chicago, Illinois, USA
Move quantum computing from laboratory systems into utility-scale infrastructure in partnership with US and allied governments
Continuously improve the modular platform as new technologies and capabilities become available
Prepare enterprises, governments, researchers, and developers for future fault-tolerant hardware through the Construct software platform
access_methods: Open-access access to the PsiQuantum Construct software platform
Publicly available/open-source and open-access software tools are described; no access method for operating PsiQuantum quantum hardware is disclosed
manufacturing_strategy: PsiQuantum designs its chips and manufactures Omega at GlobalFoundries' flagship commercial semiconductor fab in Malta, New York. The process uses standard 300 mm silicon wafers and a 45 nm lithography node. The company states that wafers are built by the thousands and that more than one million devices have been tested.
developer_tools: Python library for defining numeric and symbolic FTQC algorithms
Circuit-code generation for circuits containing billions of operations
Quantum resource estimation at FTQC scale
major_partnerships: GlobalFoundries for commercial semiconductor manufacturing in Malta, New York
DARPA through a disclosed $125 million Quantum Benchmarking Initiative agreement
US and allied governments for planned utility-scale infrastructure
Planned site development in Moreton Bay, Queensland
Planned site development at the Illinois Quantum & Microelectronics Park in Chicago
strengths: Uses established high-volume semiconductor manufacturing infrastructure rather than relying solely on small research fabs
Discloses strong component-level metrics, including 99.98% SPAM fidelity, 99.22% two-qubit fusion fidelity, and 99.72% chip-to-chip transmission fidelity
Optical-fiber networking provides a plausible modular scaling path without microwave-to-optical or other transduction
Integration of sources, detectors, and switches on the Omega platform could reduce system complexity
Photonic qubits are presented as less sensitive to heat and electromagnetic interference, allowing control electronics to be placed closer to the qubit
Construct addresses FTQC algorithm design, simulation, optimization, and resource estimation before hardware availability
Government support and the expanded DARPA agreement provide external engagement around the utility-scale roadmap
weaknesses: No physical-qubit count or complete quantum-computer scale is disclosed
No logical qubit, logical error rate, error-correction cycle, or fault-tolerant logical operation is demonstrated in the supplied material
Reported benchmarks are component- or operation-level metrics rather than evidence of an integrated utility-scale computer
The reported single-qubit metric is SPAM fidelity, not one-qubit gate fidelity
No coherence, gate-speed, photon-loss, multiplexing, system uptime, or end-to-end workload benchmark is provided
No currently operational customer-accessible quantum hardware or completed commercial deployment is identified
Planned sites and utility-scale systems remain future targets rather than demonstrated capabilities
competitive_differentiators: Foundry-manufactured silicon photonics using 300 mm wafers and a 45 nm process
Integrated Omega platform combining photon sources, superconducting detectors, and optical switching
Modular scale-out over standard telecom optical fiber without transduction
Potential colocation of control electronics near photonic qubits due to reduced heat and electromagnetic sensitivity
FTQC-focused software capable of representing and estimating circuits with very large operation counts
Explicit focus on utility-scale, fault-tolerant infrastructure rather than incremental small-system qubit-count milestones
technical_risks: Scaling strong component-level fidelities into a reliable, integrated machine may introduce compounded loss and operational errors
Two-qubit fusion fidelity of 99.22% may require substantial error-correction overhead; no threshold or overhead analysis is supplied
Photon generation, indistinguishability, routing, switching, detection, and fiber transmission must all operate concurrently at large scale
The architecture uses superconducting detectors and references operation at 10 mK, leaving cryogenic integration and scaling challenges despite the thermal advantages claimed for photons
No demonstrated logical qubits or fault-tolerant operations are disclosed, so the path from physical photonic components to useful logical computation remains unvalidated in the supplied material
The absence of disclosed gate speed, loss rates, multiplexing performance, decoder implementation, and end-to-end reliability prevents assessment of practical computational throughput
Large-scale packaging, control integration, fiber networking, and synchronization across blades and cabinets may create engineering complexity not captured by individual component benchmarks
commercialization_risks: No completed utility-scale system or current hardware-access model is disclosed
Commercial value depends on successful delivery of planned Moreton Bay and Chicago infrastructure
The capital and infrastructure requirements of utility-scale systems may limit deployment flexibility and customer access
Lack of disclosed timelines, pricing, service model, uptime, and performance commitments makes adoption readiness difficult to assess
The software platform can prepare users for FTQC, but its near-term commercial value may be constrained until compatible hardware exists
Reliance on government partnerships and large infrastructure projects may expose deployment schedules to funding, permitting, construction, and policy risks
marketing_message: PsiQuantum presents itself as moving quantum computing out of the laboratory and into utility-scale infrastructure by combining manufacturable silicon photonics, modular optical networking, integrated controls, and FTQC-focused software to build the world's first useful quantum computers.
messaging_gaps: The phrase 'world's first useful quantum computers' is aspirational in the supplied material and is not supported by a disclosed completed system or useful quantum workload
Component metrics are prominent, but their relationship to logical error rates and application-level performance is not quantified
No clear distinction is provided between demonstrated chipset capabilities and the performance of the planned full-scale computer
No delivery dates are stated for the planned Moreton Bay or Chicago systems
No explanation is provided for how customers will access, purchase, or deploy future hardware
The claimed 'beyond-state-of-the-art performance' is not accompanied by competitor-normalized comparisons in the supplied pages
data_gaps: Logical error rate and logical-qubit lifetime
One-qubit gate fidelity distinct from SPAM fidelity
Photon-loss rates across sources, switching, coupling, detection, and networking
Source brightness, repetition rate, detector efficiency, and detector dead time
Physical-qubit and hardware overhead per logical qubit
Decoder design, speed, and hardware implementation
End-to-end benchmark results on an integrated quantum computer
System availability, uptime, calibration requirements, and reliability
Current hardware access, cloud availability, and on-premises availability
Confirmed deployment dates and specifications for Moreton Bay and Chicago
Power, footprint, cryogenic, and networking requirements for a full system
Application-level quantum advantage or utility demonstration
